lesson.title: Actors and actions

steps.headline: Put the actor in the subject and the action in the verb.

lead.text: In the active voice the subject acts: “The committee rejected the motion.” The passive makes the receiver the subject: “The motion was rejected by the committee.” It builds the verb from “be” plus a past participle, and the actor moves to a “by” phrase or vanishes.
“The motion was rejected by the committee” makes the receiver its subject. Rewrite it so the committee acts, then count the words of your version.

reveal.text: You moved the actor to the front and dropped “was” and “by”. The passive's extra words disappeared, and the sentence now opens with whoever acted.

steps.headline: Make “The report was written by the analyst” active.

workedSteps.text: Find the actor. The “by” phrase names the analyst.
Make the actor the subject: “The analyst”.
Turn “was written” into a plain past verb and keep the receiver as its object: “The analyst wrote the report.”

lead.text: The passive can delete the actor altogether. That is honest when nobody knows who acted, and evasive when the writer does.

reveal.text: The actor was in the sentence all along, hidden behind “by”. Ask of every passive: who did this, and should the reader know?

steps.headline: Make “Mistakes were made by the finance office” active.

workedSteps.text: The receiver is “mistakes”, and the verb is “were made”.
The actor is named inside the “by” phrase.
Move the actor to the front. Which words become the subject?

steps.headline: A nominalisation buries a verb inside a noun.

lead.text: “Refuse” becomes “a refusal”, and “decide” becomes “a decision”. The noun then needs a weak verb such as “gave” or “made” to carry it. The sentence gains words and loses force. Turn the noun back into a verb and both come back.
Look for a noun that is really an action, and for the weak verb propping it up. Make the committee the actor.

reveal.text: You turned two noun phrases back into verbs. Fewer words, and the committee now does something.

lead.text: Some words carry no meaning a reader would miss. A phrase like “in my opinion, it is true that” only announces a claim, and a modifier can repeat what the noun already says. Count the sentence before you cut.

reveal.text: The claim stayed and ten words went. A revision that loses words and keeps the claim is an improvement you can measure.

lesson.orientation: Move actors into subjects and actions into verbs. Switch between active and passive, unbury nominalisations and count the words a revision saves.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: A shop owner finds the window smashed and asks the staff what happened.

intro.promise: By the end you'll move actors into subjects and unbury actions from nouns, counting the words each revision saves.

recap.keyIdea: Make the actor the subject and the action the verb. Unbury verbs from nouns and cut words that carry no meaning.

blocks.text: You turned a seven-word passive into five words. Unburying two verbs saved five more, and padding cut a sixteen-word sentence to six.

recap.nextHook: Clear sentences carry arguments. Next: take an argument apart into claim, grounds and warrant.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'The motion was rejected by the committee' in the active voice. How many words does the active sentence have?
hints: Make the actor, the committee, the subject.
Use the past-tense verb without 'was', and drop 'by'.
Count every word, including both articles.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five: 'The committee rejected the motion.' The passive took seven.

questions.onCorrect: Five words: “The committee rejected the motion.” The actor leads and the passive's extra words go.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the passive's own length. Rewrite it with the committee acting, then count.
Drop both “was” and “by”: the participle becomes a plain past verb.
You have lost a word. Count both articles.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'Mistakes were made by the finance office' in the active voice. What becomes the subject?
hints: Find the 'by' phrase: whoever sits inside it performed the action.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'The finance office made mistakes.' The actor, hidden in the 'by' phrase, moves into the subject position.

questions.onCorrect: The finance office made mistakes. The actor, hidden in the “by” phrase, moves into the subject.

misconceptions.feedback: “Mistakes” is the receiver. In the active sentence it follows the verb.

questions.prompt: Unbury the verbs in 'The committee made a decision to conduct a review of the policy': 'made a decision' becomes 'decided' and 'conduct a review of' becomes 'review'. How many words does the revision save?
hints: Count the words in the original sentence.
Write out the revision and count it.
Subtract the revised count from the original count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Twelve words become seven: 'The committee decided to review the policy.' Five are saved.

questions.onCorrect: Twelve words become seven, so the revision saves five. Buried verbs cost words and force.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the original length. The question asks how many words the revision saves.
That is the length of the revision. Subtract it from the original.
Recount each sentence one word at a time, then check the subtraction.

questions.prompt: Cut the empty frame 'In my opinion, it is true that' and the redundant words 'personal', 'basically' and 'final' from 'In my personal opinion, it is basically true that the final outcome depends on the weather.' How many words remain?
hints: Count the original sentence first.
Count the frame words and the redundant words you are removing.
Subtract, then check by reading what is left aloud.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sixteen words lose ten: 'The outcome depends on the weather.' Six remain.

questions.onCorrect: Six words remain: sixteen lose ten. Cutting padding keeps the claim and loses only noise.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the words you cut. Count what is left.
That is the original length. Remove the frame and the repeated words first.
Check that you removed every word listed, including the three modifiers.

questions.prompt: 'The budget was approved by the council in March.' How many words does the active version save?
hints: Put the council in the subject position.
Write the active sentence and count it.
Subtract the active count from the passive count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nine words become seven: 'The council approved the budget in March.' Two are saved.

questions.onCorrect: Nine words become seven, so two are saved. Moving the actor forward drops “was” and “by”.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the passive's own length. Count the active version and subtract.
That is the active sentence's length. The question asks how many words are saved.

questions.prompt: 'An investigation of the causes was carried out by the board.' Which verb is buried inside the noun 'investigation'?
hints: Remove the noun ending '-ation' and rebuild the verb.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Investigate': 'The board investigated the causes' turns the noun back into a verb and the board into the subject.

questions.onCorrect: “Investigation” hides the verb “investigate”. Turn it back and the board becomes the actor.

misconceptions.feedback: “Carried out” is the weak verb propping the noun up. Look inside the noun itself.

questions.prompt: Which sentence tells you who broke the window?
hints: Which sentence would let you ask “Who?” and get an answer?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “Sam broke the window.” names the actor.

questions.onCorrect: Only the first names the person who acted. In the others the window comes first and the actor disappears.

misconceptions.feedback: That sentence is complete, but it never says who did it.
“Got broken” hides the actor just as the other passive does.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
hints: Ask whether the subject does the action or receives it.

acceptedIdeas: The pitch was flooded by the storm.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pitch was flooded by the storm.

choices.label: The pitch was flooded by the storm.

questions.onCorrect: In the passive the receiver is the subject, and the verb is “be” plus a past participle.

misconceptions.feedback: Here the storm is the subject and it acts, so the sentence is active.
“Was fierce” links the storm to a description. No action is received, so it is not passive.

questions.prompt: Why does the active version read as stronger?

acceptedIdeas: The reader meets the actor first, and the verb is shorter.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The actor leads and the verb is shorter.

choices.label: The reader meets the actor first, and the verb is shorter.
It is longer, so it carries more detail.

questions.onCorrect: The actor leads and the verb is direct, so the sentence says who did what in fewer words.

misconceptions.feedback: It is shorter, not longer. The extra words in the passive carry nothing.
Not always. The passive suits cases where the actor is unknown or does not matter.

questions.prompt: Which sentence puts the actor in the subject and the action in the verb: “A review of the rules was undertaken by the staff”?
hints: Two things have to change: who leads, and where the action sits.

choices.label: The staff undertook a review of the rules.
The rules were reviewed by the staff.

questions.onCorrect: “Reviewed” turns the buried noun back into a verb, and the staff acts as subject.

misconceptions.feedback: The staff are now the subject, but the action is still buried in a noun.
The verb is restored, but the sentence is still passive, so the receiver leads.

questions.prompt: Which sentence buries its verb in a noun?
hints: Look for an action word that has become a noun, propped up by a weak verb.

acceptedIdeas: The board gave a refusal of the request.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The board gave a refusal of the request.

choices.label: The board gave a refusal of the request.

questions.onCorrect: “A refusal” is the action turned into a noun, and “gave” is a weak verb carrying it.

misconceptions.feedback: “Refused” is the action as a verb, so nothing is buried here.
“Was long” describes the request. No action is hidden in a noun.
